gaps.sentence: There's ___ at the door — go and see who it is.
gaps.explanation: 'Somebody' is used in affirmative sentences for an unknown person; 'anybody' belongs to questions and negatives.

gaps.sentence: The night bus runs ___ twenty minutes.
gaps.explanation: 'Every twenty minutes' expresses regular intervals; 'each twenty minutes' is not used.

gaps.sentence: ___ of what he says is nonsense.
gaps.explanation: 'Most of what he says' is the pattern 'most of + noun clause'; 'the most of' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: She gave the children two sweets ___.
gaps.hint: distribution per child at the end of the sentence
gaps.explanation: 'Two sweets each' means two per child; 'every' cannot stand alone here.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the milk has gone off, so do not drink it.
gaps.explanation: 'All of the milk' — 'whole' would need 'the whole of the milk'.

gaps.sentence: There is ___ milk in the fridge — help yourself.
gaps.hint: affirmative statement; the invitation confirms it
gaps.explanation: 'Some milk' fits the affirmative statement and the invitation; 'no milk' would contradict 'help yourself'.

gaps.sentence: I haven't got ___ cash on me — I'll pay by card.
gaps.explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in negative sentences; 'haven't got no cash' would be a double negative.

gaps.sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
gaps.hint: one of a pair of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.
